core_obligations: Reduce to the adic* case, using that Noetherianness implies the adic* property and the corresponding two-way statement (proof lines 4661-4665).
Invoke the Noetherianness criterion and write the target as a countable colimit of affine schemes as in the presentation lemma (proof lines 4665-4668).

Base change the morphism to each stage: the result is an affine scheme because the morphism is representable and affine, the stages present the source, and each induced morphism is faithfully flat and of finite type (proof lines 4668-4677).
Conclude in both directions from the algebra statements on Noetherianness under faithfully flat finite type maps (proof lines 4677-4679).
proof_roadmap: Reduction to the adic* case (proof lines 4661-4665).
Stages of the target and their base changes (proof lines 4665-4677).
Conclusion by the two algebra statements (proof lines 4677-4679).
difficulty_reason: For a morphism of affine formal algebraic spaces which is representable, surjective, flat and locally of finite type, the lemma asserts that the source is Noetherian if and only if the target is (statement lines 4654-4659). The proof first observes that a Noetherian affine formal algebraic space is adic*, so that by the corresponding statement for the adic* property one may assume both spaces are adic* (proof lines 4661-4665). It then invokes the criterion for Noetherianness of such a space, writes the target as a countable colimit as in the corresponding presentation lemma, base changes the morphism to each stage -- which is an affine scheme because the morphism is representable and affine -- and notes that the stages present the source as a colimit and that each induced morphism of stages is faithfully flat and of finite type (proof lines 4667-4677). The conclusion follows from the two algebra statements giving that Noetherianness ascends and descends along such a ring map (proof lines 4677-4679). The claim is H2: the argument reduces one type to another, then applies a criterion to convert the geometric statement into a statement about the stages, where the two directions are the two cited algebra statements.
